paragraphs: You’ll be glad to hear that nothing has gone wrong at the start of an enterprise you viewed with such dark misgivings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first task is to reassure my dear sister that I am well and growing more confident that this will succeed.

I am already far north of London, and as I walk the streets of Petersburg, I feel a cold northern breeze on my cheeks that steadies my nerves and fills me with delight. Do you understand this feeling? This breeze, which has traveled from the regions I am heading toward, gives me a foretaste of those icy lands. Inspired by this promising wind, my daydreams grow more ardent and vivid. I try in vain to convince myself that the pole is a place of frost and desolation. In my imagination it always appears as a region of beauty and delight. There, Margaret, the sun is always visible, its broad disk just skimming the horizon and spreading a never-ending splendor. There (with your permission, sister, I’ll put some trust in the navigators who came before me) snow and frost are banished, and sailing over a calm sea, we may be carried to a land surpassing in wonder and beauty every region yet discovered on the habitable globe. Its products and features may be like nothing known, just as the movements of the heavenly bodies surely are in those undiscovered solitudes. What might we not expect in a country of eternal light? I may discover there the marvelous power that attracts the compass needle, and I may settle a thousand astronomical observations that need only this voyage to make their apparent oddities consistent for all time. I will satisfy my burning curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never visited before, and may tread on land never touched by a human foot. These are my attractions, and they are enough to overcome all fear of danger or death and to make me begin this laborious voyage with the joy a child feels when he sets out in a little boat with his holiday friends on an expedition of discovery up his native river. But suppose all these guesses are wrong. You cannot deny the immense benefit I would bring to all mankind, down to the last generation, by discovering a passage near the pole to those countries that now take so many months to reach, or by uncovering the secret of the magnet, which, if it can be done at all, can only be done by an undertaking like mine.

These reflections have calmed the agitation I felt when I began my letter, and I feel my heart glow with an enthusiasm that lifts me to heaven, because nothing steadies the mind so much as a firm purpose, a point on which the soul can fix its gaze. This expedition has been the favorite dream of my early years. I have read eagerly about the many voyages made in hopes of reaching the North Pacific Ocean through the seas around the pole. You may remember that a history of all the voyages of discovery made up the whole of our good Uncle Thomas’s library. My education was neglected, yet I was passionately fond of reading. Those volumes were my study day and night, and my familiarity with them deepened the regret I had felt as a child, when I learned that my father’s dying wish had forbidden my uncle to let me take up a life at sea.

These visions faded when I first read those poets whose outpourings enchanted my soul and lifted it to heaven. I became a poet myself and for one year lived in a paradise of my own making. I imagined I might win a place in the temple where the names of Homer and Shakespeare are enshrined. You know well how I failed and how heavily I bore the disappointment. But just then I inherited my cousin’s fortune, and my thoughts turned back to their earlier course.

Six years have passed since I resolved on my present undertaking. Even now I can remember the hour from which I dedicated myself to this great enterprise. I began by toughening my body against hardship. I accompanied whale fishermen on several expeditions to the North Sea. I willingly endured cold, hunger, thirst, and lack of sleep. I often worked harder than the ordinary sailors during the day and gave my nights to the study of mathematics, the theory of medicine, and those branches of physical science from which a naval adventurer might gain the greatest practical advantage. Twice I actually hired on as an under-mate on a Greenland whaler and acquitted myself admirably. I must admit I felt a little proud when my captain offered me the second-highest position on the ship and begged me earnestly to stay, so valuable did he consider my services.

And now, dear Margaret, don’t I deserve to accomplish some great purpose? My life might have been spent in ease and luxury, but I preferred glory to every temptation that wealth put in my path. Oh, if only some encouraging voice would answer yes! My courage and my resolve are firm, but my hopes waver and my spirits are often low. I am about to set off on a long and difficult voyage, whose emergencies will demand all my strength. I am required not only to lift the spirits of others, but sometimes to keep up my own when theirs are failing.

This is the best time of year for traveling in Russia. They fly quickly over the snow in their sleighs. The motion is pleasant and, in my opinion, far more agreeable than an English stagecoach. The cold isn’t excessive if you’re wrapped in furs, a style of dress I have already adopted, because there’s a great difference between walking the deck and sitting motionless for hours with no exercise to keep the blood from freezing in your veins. I have no ambition to lose my life on the post road between St. Petersburg and Archangel.

I will leave for that town in a fortnight or three weeks. My plan is to hire a ship there, which is easily done by paying the owner’s insurance, and to sign on as many sailors as I think necessary from among those used to whale fishing. I don’t intend to sail until June. And when will I return? Ah, dear sister, how can I answer that? If I succeed, many, many months, perhaps years, will pass before you and I can meet. If I fail, you will see me again soon, or never.
Farewell, my dear, excellent Margaret. May Heaven shower blessings on you and keep me safe, so that I may again and again show my gratitude for all your love and kindness.
